supporting_texts: FAO (1978, p.  1) originally adopted the term "community forestry" as an umbrella term for "any situation which intimately involves local people in a forestry activity".

FAO (2012b) has defined participatory forestry as: "processes and mechanisms which enable people with a direct stake in forest resources to be part of decision-making in all aspects of forest management, including policy formulation processes".

FAO (2010a, pp. 236−237) recorded them as being forests where "communities" are the "holder(s) of management rights of public forests".  FAO (2012b, p. 41) noted that CBF emerged in the Asia and the Pacific region, in part, "in the context of failures by public forestry organizations to effectively protect and manage forests sustainably".  The emergence, growth and evolution of community‑based forestry ... can be traced back to the seminal paper Forestry for local community development (FAO, 1978).
FAO's Forests, Trees and People Programme (FTPP), with its regional hubs, was an important platform for developing and supporting networks to exchange information and share experiences.

actors.name: France
actors.description: European nation whose public forests are managed by local government authorities rather than discrete community groups.
actors.role: Serves as an example of a country where communal management rights exist but are administered by state authorities, illustrating limited inclusion of true community‑based forestry regimes.
actors.supporting_text: France and Switzerland remain the only two countries in Europe in which significant areas of the forest estate are managed through some form of communal management rights (FAO, 2010a). However, in both these countries the commune forests are public forests managed by local government authorities and not by discrete community groups.

significance.justification: Illustrates limited presence of communal rights within Europe.
significance.supporting_text: France ... where significant areas ... are managed through some form of communal management rights.

actors.name: Elinor Ostrom
actors.description: Scholar whose 1990 work popularized the narrative that local communities can autonomously manage forest commons sustainably.
actors.role: Provided the foundational theoretical narrative that underpins community‑based forestry, arguing that granted property rights enable local institutions to regulate and manage natural resources sustainably.
actors.supporting_text: The popularity of community-based forestry as a formal type of forestry rests primarily on a narrative popularized by Ostrom (1990) that local communities, when granted sufficient property rights over local forest commons, can organize autonomously and develop local institutions to regulate the use of natural resources and manage them sustainably.

significance.justification: Her narrative underpins the idea that communities can self‑organize for sustainable forest use.
significance.supporting_text: Narrative popularized by Ostrom (1990) that local communities … can organize autonomously … and manage them sustainably.

actors.supporting_text: Tole (2010, p. 1312) noted that CBF initiatives "fit squarely within the larger economy wide and institutional reforms that many governments have been pursuing under IMF [International Monetary Fund] and World Bank conditionality lending since the 1990s.

significance.justification: Links CBF to IMF/World Bank conditionality and government downsizing of services.
